overview: Makkura is the map’s name for Makuria. Its capital, Dongola, grew around a fortified centre beside the Nile. Houses, churches and workshops reveal a city of builders and makers as well as rulers.

periods.title: A fortified capital and a Christian kingdom
periods.summary: Dongola’s citadel developed around the late fifth century. The kingdom adopted Christianity in the sixth century, and the city expanded beyond its walls. The map’s opening at 500 is approximate coverage.

periods.title: Independence, diplomacy and exchange
periods.summary: After conflict with forces from Egypt in 651/652, arrangements known as the baqt shaped relations and exchanges. These involved goods and enslaved people. Makuria maintained its independence; the details and interpretation of the arrangements remain subjects of historical debate.

periods.title: Religious buildings and political change
periods.summary: Dongola’s buildings were repeatedly adapted. A monumental hall interpreted as a royal audience building suffered late-thirteenth-century destruction and rebuilding. An Arabic inscription dates its conversion into a mosque to 1317.

periods.title: After the court left Dongola
periods.summary: The court departed in the 1360s, followed by Makuria’s fragmentation. Dongola continued as a smaller kingdom and later entered the Funj sphere. Households and settlement persisted through political and religious change.

periods.title: Research into everyday lives
periods.summary: Modern research combines excavated objects and buildings with scientific analysis. Traces preserved in floors can reveal domestic activities even where few tools or furnishings survived.

items.text: House A at Old Dongola had a bathroom with heated water and painted walls, plus a toilet upstairs. These excavated features show that some residents devoted considerable effort to comfort and sanitation. An upstairs toilet belongs in the history of medieval engineering too. This particular house does not tell us that every family enjoyed the same facilities.

A study of four Dongola house compounds, spanning the fourteenth to seventeenth centuries, examined chemical traces in floors. Comparisons with reference samples helped locate activities, especially food preparation, where few visible objects remained. A swept floor can still hold clues. The researchers found that similar-looking homes could be used in different ways as residents’ needs changed.

From the fourteenth century onward, many Dongola dwellings grouped small residential buildings around a shared courtyard. Rooms included benches and storage spaces for vessels and equipment. Archaeologists examine how shared and separate working areas shaped household relationships. A floor plan can suggest how people met and worked together, but it cannot establish every resident’s family tree.

sections.title: Learning, writing and keeping track of things

items.text: A rubbish deposit beside Dongola’s monastery church contained pottery fragments used for writing exercises. Examples include a Coptic alphabet and archangels’ names written in an unpractised hand. Other pieces carry Greek grammar exercises. Broken pottery could serve as a writing surface. These finds show learning, although they do not reveal every pupil’s age or how many children attended lessons.

A monastery room yielded two groups of dishes bearing the names of religious leaders Lazaros and Stephanos. Each group included roughly ten pots. Writing could identify belongings as well as record prayers. These names connect ordinary tableware with particular people, though the finds do not prove whether each leader ate alone or shared meals with others.

Some Dongola inscriptions switch between Greek and Old Nubian. Other texts present psalms in both languages, sometimes alternating the language from verse to verse. This makes multilingual religious life visible on the walls. The texts preserve written choices, but they do not tell us that every resident spoke both languages fluently.

A land-sale document from Qasr Ibrim names a woman, Kapopi, selling property inherited from her mother to Neuesi, an official’s daughter, and Anenikoli. A 2019 reanalysis dates it to November 1, 1191, while noting an older discussion using 1190. This northern Nubian record preserves a woman acting in a property transaction, without proving that every woman had identical rights or wealth.

Old Nubian land sales often described a plot by naming neighbouring owners and the land upstream and downstream along the Nile. The 2019 study argues that descriptions normally proceed from south to north. Finding your field depended on relationships between people and places: the neighbours were part of the address. Some readings and exact locations remain uncertain.

A pot beneath the pavement of the church on Kom D at Dongola contained a necklace of about one hundred beads. Materials included coloured glass, faience, shell, bone and stone. Researchers interpreted it as a seventh-century foundation deposit. The necklace shows materials brought together in an unusual setting; its placement does not tell us who previously wore it, or whether anyone did.

Dongola ornaments included marine shells altered for suspension. Some cowrie shells had their upper surfaces removed or pierced; larger cone shells had their tips cut off. One pierced shell still had a leather thong. These objects connect inland adornment with marine materials and skilled preparation, while the route taken by each shell remains unknown.

sections.title: Buildings that changed purpose, and discoveries today

items.text: Dongola’s Mosque Building preserves an Arabic foundation inscription dated 1317. Architectural study shows the earlier monumental hall being adapted for worship, including a prayer niche and new plaster over painted walls. Its earlier role as a royal audience hall is an interpretation of its plan and decoration. One building’s conversion did not mean that every resident changed religion that year.

In a discovery announced in 2023, archaeologists investigating a later house found an opening into a small painted chamber below its floor. One scene shows a Nubian ruler with Christ and Archangel Michael. Preliminary reading of a difficult inscription mentions a King David and protection for a city. The identification and historical occasion were still being investigated: a dramatic painting is not a photograph of a known event.

ending.text: Makuria fragmented during the fourteenth and fifteenth centuries. The court left Dongola in the 1360s, but the city continued under a smaller kingdom and later within the Funj sphere. Changes of government and religion unfolded over time. The map’s 1492 endpoint does not establish a single conquest or the disappearance of Nubian communities.
